content: To effectively assess and validate program performance, including its impact, it is essential to employ triangulation methods and specialized studies. A simplified and standardized methodology is critical to ensure a consistent approach to these reviews. Public health sector staff and partners at various levels of the health system can contribute to this process as appropriate. The foundation of this approach is a prioritized, straightforward set of selected indicators that can be analyzed at national, subnational, and facility levels. National program managers should conduct routine data reviews at least annually, and ideally more frequently, focusing on fundamental geographic divisions (e.g., subnational, facility levels) and disaggregating data by age, gender, and key populations. This allows for the identification of disparities in service access (coverage) and quality. Subnational area managers, such as those at provincial or district levels, may perform more frequent reviews (e.g., quarterly), while facility managers might review their data even more often (e.g., monthly). These reviews help monitor progress and support staff in delivering services more efficiently and effectively. The transition from aggregate to individual-level data enables patient-centered monitoring and case surveillance. Individual-level data, as captured in primary data collection tools like patient charts, are vital for patient care and monitoring. As countries implement Treat All policies, patient-level data become increasingly important for ensuring effective, high-quality services. The quality of individual-level data offers a significant advantage over aggregate data, driving investments in digital health information systems. For instance, electronic medical records (EMRs) support person-centered care and patient monitoring while serving as a source for aggregate reporting of service indicator data. HIV case surveillance is a critical component of program management, utilizing a subset of individual-level data linked by unique identifiers. This data facilitates accountability and program management objectives. The 2017 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance identify five sentinel events in the HIV care cascade that must be monitored as a minimal data set for effective case surveillance: HIV diagnosis, initiation of antiretroviral treatment (ART), viral load testing, viral load suppression, and death. When combined with dates and robust unique identification standards, these data can be transformed into key indicators to identify gaps in the care cascade. Integrating and aligning components of these systems, such as linking electronic patient monitoring systems to case surveillance data repositories or aggregate reporting systems, allows countries to benefit from the efficiency of a common data source. This approach supports three fundamental data functions: patient care, program management, and program monitoring. The principle is collect once, use many times. Similarly, tracking the delivery of prevention services (e.g., condoms, harm reduction services, PrEP) to individuals benefits from individual-level data and unique identification. While aggregate counts of service delivery can be challenging to deduplicate, individual-level data allow for deduplication but may increase reporting burdens. The delivery of HIV prevention, care, and treatment services depends on the capability of the underlying health system. WHO has defined six building blocks of functional health services: service delivery infrastructure, the health workforce, medical products and technology, financing, health information systems, and leadership and governance. Monitoring the status and performance of these building blocks is a prerequisite for providing HIV services. Deficiencies in any of these key system components, particularly the health workforce, will immediately affect the system's capacity to deliver, monitor, and manage HIV program services. In many countries, the availability of health system data, especially at the facility level, is often limited or not robust. Monitoring health system data, such as human resources and the supply chain, is vital for interpreting service cascade data and managing responses to related data analyses. These system data should be included in routine data review activities, and the information systems that provide these data should be prioritized in planning and resource allocation. Routine data reviews should be a core function of program managers at every level. Establishing such a process involves convening program managers, including civil society, community representatives, and development partners, to review data at specified intervals. It also requires developing a simple, standardized core analysis plan for routine data that informs management decisions at different levels, acting on findings to adjust service delivery, supervision, and resource allocation, and tracking the effects of these adjustments over time through ongoing routine data review. Managers at different levels require different types of strategic information to inform their decisions. For example, facility-level managers may review data monthly or more frequently to track outreach prevention services, improve testing yield and linkage to ART, optimize ART retention, and achieve viral load suppression. District or regional managers may conduct quarterly reviews to forecast service and resource needs, prioritize bottlenecks, and assess performance against targets. National-level managers may review data annually or more frequently to identify highand low-performing areas, assess equity in service coverage and outcomes, and track progress toward national strategy goals. To facilitate routine data reviews focused on the service cascade, national programs can develop data dashboards for standardized display of analytic outputs, including figures, tables, and maps accessible to managers at different levels. These dashboards should focus on a select set of indicators to ensure feasibility and effectiveness.
